verses.translation_literal: On the rivers of Babylon, there we sat; also we wept, in our remembering Zion.
verses.translation_dramatic: By the rivers of Babylon we sat down, and there, on the strange bank, we wept. Every time we remembered Zion, the water went on running, and we had nothing to answer it with but tears.
verses.directors_commentary: Play this as a group, not a soloist: the whole verse is first-person plural, 'we sat… we wept… we remembered', the voice of the exiles together, and the Levite singers of the Temple are the speakers according to Ibn Ezra and Radak. The scene is geography, and the geography is Babylonian: 'rivers' (plural) in the flat canal country of the Tigris and Euphrates, where irrigation canals ran through the land the deportees were settled on. Jerusalem had one spring, the Gihon; Ibn Ezra uses exactly this contrast to prove that the speakers are standing in Babylon. Sitting is the body language of mourning (Lam 2:10), and Ibn Ezra hears in 'sat' the sense of being stunned, 'desolate', which is why the Hebrew adds גַּם 'also': they did not only sit, they also wept. KJV 'yea, we wept' makes that 'also' an exclamation of intensity; the Hebrew simply adds the second action. 'When we remembered' is one word in Hebrew (בְּזָכְרֵנוּ, 'in our remembering'), an infinitive: the weeping and the remembering are the same moment, and the object marker אֶת־ before Zion gives the name weight. Note too the sound: the verse's verbs are all in the sound -נו, 'we', and the piece ends on Zion, the one word that is not 'we'. Malbim stresses that the grief was spiritual, not economic: Jeremiah 29:5 told them to build houses and plant vineyards, and they did, and still wept.

philological_notes.note: 'We sat' is also the verb for 'dwell', so the line holds both 'we sat down' and 'we lived there': Malbim hears 'a settled sitting', Ibn Ezra a stunned, desolate sitting (like Lam 1:1 and the participle 'sits desolate').
A prepositional infinitive, 'in our remembering': the weeping is simultaneous with the memory. Ibn Ezra reads 'I will forget you' in v. 5 as the answer to this 'remembering'.

verses.translation_literal: On poplars in the midst of it we hung our lyres.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the poplars that stood in the midst of that land we hung our harps, and left them there, swaying silent in the branches.
verses.directors_commentary: A short, hard image: the instruments are not smashed or thrown, they are hung up, as a worker hangs a tool he will not use. The traditional readings split on why. Radak says the singers laid the instruments aside out of grief; Metzudat David says they hid them in the branches so the enemy would not see them; Malbim says that even in a land of pleasant things they refused joy. For a Levite the כִּנּוֹר (kinnor) is not a pastime; it is the temple instrument, the one David played, played with the right hand over the strings, which is why v. 5 turns to the right hand. KJV 'willows' is the first mistranslation: עֲרָבִים are most likely the Euphrates poplar (Populus euphratica) that lines Mesopotamian canals; Rashi and Radak identify them with the 'brook willows' of Lev 23:40, and the reader should hear a riverside tree, whichever the species. KJV also reads 'in the midst thereof' as if it modified the willows ('in the midst thereof' = in the midst of the land); the Hebrew 'in the midst of it' has a feminine suffix, which Ibn Ezra and Radak read as Babylon. Ibn Ezra disagrees with Moses ha-Kohen, who read it as 'in Zion', and decides for Babylon because of the rivers in v. 1. Kinnor is 'lyre', not the large European harp the English word suggests: a small hand-held instrument with an arm and a crossbar, light enough to hang from a branch.

philological_notes.note: Trees that grow by water; the Euphrates poplar is the usual modern identification, 'willow' (KJV) is traditional. Rashi and Metzudat Zion link the word to 'brook willows' (עַרְבֵי נַחַל, Lev 23:40).
The kinnor, a hand-held lyre, the instrument of the Levitical singers; 'harps' (KJV) is an old English rendering that suggests a different, larger instrument.

verses.translation_literal: For there our captors asked us for words of a song, and those who mock us [asked] gladness: 'Sing for us from a song of Zion.'
verses.translation_dramatic: For there, on that very bank, the men who had led us off in chains asked us for a song. Our tormentors wanted laughter from us. 'Sing us one of the songs of Zion,' they said.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the scene turns from silence to pressure. The speakers are prisoners of war, and the verse says so in one word: שׁוֹבֵינוּ, 'our captors' (literally 'those who took us captive'). The request is not innocent. The first half asks for 'words of a song'; the second half asks for 'gladness', that is, entertainment from the defeated. Play the voices of the captors with a smile. 'Songs of Zion' are the songs sung at the Temple in praise of the city and its God, so the request is also a taunt: sing the songs of the God who has just lost. Malbim hears the demand as a request to sing in praise of the land they now live in, as they once sang of Jerusalem.

The hardest word is תוֹלָלֵינוּ, found only here, and the tradition gives three answers. First, instruments that are 'hung': Rashi's first reading (after Menahem), Ibn Ezra, who glosses 'ותוללינו' as 'our hung things, the instruments of joy', and Radak, who paraphrases the verse as 'they asked us to rejoice with our lyres that we hung on the poplars'. That reading would echo 'we hung' in v. 2. Second, 'our mockers' from הלל: Rashi's second reading (citing Ps 102:9, 'those who rage against me'), Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion. Third, 'our wailing' from ילל: Meiri ('in the midst of our wailing they asked us for gladness'), and the view Radak cites as 'some interpret', that of Moses ha-Kohen, whom Ibn Ezra rejects. I render 'those who mock us' because it matches 'our captors' as a parallel and the tone of the request, and I leave the other readings in the note. KJV 'they that wasted us' follows the Targum's 'plundered us' and is hard to defend from the Hebrew. KJV and ASV also supply 'required' twice; Hebrew uses one verb, 'asked', for both halves. The captors speak directly: 'Sing for us from a song of Zion', literally 'from the song', that is, a sample, any one.

philological_notes.note: A hapax legomenon, read three ways. 'Our hung [instruments]': Rashi's first reading (from Menahem), Ibn Ezra, Radak. 'Our mockers' (from הלל): Rashi's second reading, Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion. 'Our wailing' (from ילל): Meiri, and the 'some interpret' cited by Radak (Moses ha-Kohen, rejected by Ibn Ezra). The Targum renders 'those who plundered us', which KJV follows.
Participle 'those who took us captive'; Metzudat Zion links it to שְׁבִי, captivity. KJV 'they that carried us away captive' is correct.
'Sing from a song of Zion': the prefix מִן is partitive, so the demand is for one sample, not the whole repertoire. KJV 'one of the songs' is right here.

verses.translation_literal: How shall we sing the song of YHWH on the soil of a foreigner?
verses.translation_dramatic: How could we? How shall we sing the song of the LORD on soil that belongs to a stranger?
verses.directors_commentary: This is the exiles' answer, and it is one short question, 'How?' (אֵיךְ). The word is the short form of אֵיכָה, the word that opens Lamentations, the cry over the fallen city. Play it as inability, not defiance: the words are not 'we will not' but 'how can we?'. The difference matters. They refuse to turn the song of YHWH into entertainment, and they say why: the song belongs to a place. The divine name stands in a construct chain, 'song of YHWH', which makes it a sacred song, set against the 'song of Zion' that the captors asked for in v. 3; the speakers silently change the term. 'Soil of a foreigner' (אַדְמַת נֵכָר) is literally 'ground of foreignness': אֲדָמָה is the farmland and the territory of a god, and in the ancient Near East a god was thought bound to his own land and temple. Ibn Ezra and Radak add a second reading, 'ground of a foreign god', the opposite of the song of YHWH; Malbim says the holy song needs the Shekhinah and the Temple, which a foreign land lacks. KJV 'strange land' is archaic and misleading: 'strange' today means odd, while נֵכָר means foreign and alien, belonging to someone else. Metzudat David makes it concrete: they feared being forced to sing, and so they hid the instruments in v. 2.

philological_notes.note: 'Soil of foreignness': a construct of 'ground' and 'the foreign'. Ibn Ezra and Radak also read it as 'ground of a foreign god', as the opposite of 'song of YHWH'.
'How?', the short form of אֵיכָה, the word that opens Lamentations (Lam 1:1). It is the question of lament and of impossibility, not a request for method.

verses.translation_literal: If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget.
verses.translation_dramatic: If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget what it knows.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice turns from 'we' to 'I' and from the captors to the city itself: Jerusalem is addressed, 'you', as a person. Ibn Ezra says each of the singers says this in his own heart; Rashi gives it to the congregation of Israel. It is an oath in the classic self-curse form: 'if I do X, may Y happen to me', with the curse left unstated in the first half. The curse here is peculiarly exact: the right hand is the hand that plucks the lyre (Ibn Ezra, Radak), so the singer swears by the thing he has just hung up. There is a verbal echo to be played: 'forget' appears twice in two Hebrew words, אֶשְׁכָּחֵךְ … תִּשְׁכַּח, and Ibn Ezra notes that it answers 'remembering' in v. 1. The second clause has no object. KJV and ASV supply 'her cunning' or 'skill' and BBE 'the memory of its art'; the Hebrew simply says 'may my right hand forget', and the reader has to decide what: its skill, its strength, or perhaps to be withered, as some commentators say (Ibn Ezra reports an opinion that the verb means 'dry up'; Meiri 'lose its power entirely'). Leave it open on stage: the actor should let the unfinished line hang. Also note that KJV 'cunning' meant skill in 1611; today it suggests deceit.

philological_notes.note: 'May my right hand forget': the verb has no object. Understood as forgetting the playing (Radak), losing all strength (Meiri, Metzudat David), or withering (an opinion cited by Ibn Ezra).

verses.translation_literal: May my tongue cleave to my palate if I do not remember you, if I do not lift up Jerusalem above the head of my joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my tongue cling to the roof of my mouth, silent forever, if I do not remember you. Let it, if I do not raise Jerusalem above the very crown of my joy.
verses.directors_commentary: The oath continues with a second self-curse, this time on the tongue, the singer's other instrument. The curse comes first this time: 'may my tongue cleave to my palate' is followed by the two conditions, 'if I do not remember you… if I do not lift up Jerusalem'. Where the hand loses its power to play, the tongue loses its power to sing (Ibn Ezra and Radak: the tongue is the organ of singing). The sound is the plain physical image of a dry mouth that cannot speak; the Hebrew does not soften it. The key phrase is עַל רֹאשׁ שִׂמְחָתִי, 'above the head of my joy'. 'Head' can mean the top or chief (KJV 'my chief joy') or the beginning: Metzudat David reads it as 'at the start of the joy', and Rashi, citing Bava Batra 60b, reads 'lift up' as bringing up the memory of the destruction at the head of every celebration. KJV 'prefer' is a paraphrase: the verb is אַעֲלֶה, 'raise, lift', a verb of going up (the same verb of 'going up' to Jerusalem), and the idea is of lifting a thing up above one's own head. Note the change of 'you': v. 5 says 'forget you' (feminine suffix, spoken to the city); v. 6 repeats it with the long spelling אֶזְכְּרֵכִי, an archaic form of the feminine 'you' that gives the line a solemn, archaic sound, to be played slowly. On who is speaking, Meiri reads vv. 5-6 as the Levite's apology: he sang under compulsion, from the hand that ruled over them, and not from the heart. Radak notes that the Levites' words end here, and that the last three verses, 7-9, are the psalmist's own.

philological_notes.note: 'Lift up above the head of my joy': 'head' as top or chief (KJV) or as start (Metzudat David); Rashi reads 'raise' as raising the memory of the destruction at the head of joy. Metzudat Zion takes על ראש as equal to בראש 'at the head'.
An archaic long form of the feminine suffix -כִי, 'I will remember you' (fem.); Ibn Ezra reads it as remembering in speech, as in 'you shall no more mention' (Jer 23:36).

verses.translation_literal: Remember, YHWH, to the sons of Edom, the day of Jerusalem, those who say: 'Lay bare, lay bare, down to the foundation in it!'
verses.translation_dramatic: Remember, O LORD, what the sons of Edom did on the day of Jerusalem. Remember how they cried out: 'Strip it! Strip it bare, down to its very foundations!'
verses.directors_commentary: The memory that began as the exiles' grief becomes a prayer that God will remember too, and the same verb, זכר, 'remember', that opened the psalm in v. 1 is now turned toward God and against Edom. Edom is the brother nation, descended from Esau, which stood by and cheered when Jerusalem fell (compare Obadiah 10-14, Lam 4:21, Ezek 35). Ibn Ezra insists that this is not about Rome and Titus, as many believed, because the next verse names Babylon; it is the Chaldean destruction of 587/586 BC, when Edomites urged the Babylonians on. 'The day of Jerusalem' is the day of its fall, and the Hebrew is blunt: a single day, a day with a name. The Edomites' cry is a doubled imperative, עָרוּ עָרוּ, from the verb עָרָה, 'to strip bare, to make naked': Rashi connects it to 'laying bare the foundation' in Hab 3:13, the uprooting of something to its roots. Keep the doubling in performance: it is a chant, a shout taken up by a crowd. KJV 'rase it' is an obsolete spelling of 'raze', and 'in the day of Jerusalem' is ambiguous: KJV 'remember… the children of Edom in the day' sounds like a favor to Edom; ASV 'against the children of Edom' gets the sense right, and Hebrew לִבְנֵי אֱדוֹם 'to/against the sons of Edom' has the sense of 'on the account of' (Metzudat David: 'to repay them'). The final בָּהּ, 'in it', is the city (feminine), so 'down to its foundation' has the sense of digging down inside the city to its base.

philological_notes.note: A doubled imperative, 'strip bare!': the verb means to make naked or lay bare, and describes demolition down to the foundation (Rashi cites Jer 51:58 and Hab 3:13; Metzudat Zion also cites Hab 3). Ibn Ezra relates it to 'pour out' (יערה) in a shorter form.
'The day of Jerusalem' is its day of destruction, as 'day of Midian' (Isa 9:3) and 'day of the LORD' name a decisive day. Radak glosses it 'the day of the destruction of Jerusalem'.

verses.translation_literal: Daughter of Babylon, the devastated one: blessed [is] he who repays to you your dealing that you dealt to us.
verses.translation_dramatic: Daughter of Babylon, you who are marked for ruin: blessed is the one who pays you back in full for what you did to us.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns directly on the enemy and speaks to her. 'Daughter of Babylon' is a personification: cities and peoples are 'daughters' (Daughter Zion, Daughter Edom), and the title is both tender and contemptuous, as when the prophets mock a fallen 'virgin daughter'. Ibn Ezra calls it the poet's prayer that she be devastated; Radak and Meiri say it is a prophecy of her fall to Darius the Mede, and Malbim says Cyrus had already plundered her. The participle הַשְּׁדוּדָה, 'the one who is devastated', can mean 'already ruined' or 'doomed to be ruined', which is why translators split ('who art to be destroyed', KJV; 'the devastated one', YLT); the Hebrew has no tense and I keep the passive. The blessing formula אַשְׁרֵי, 'how blessed', is the opening of Psalm 1, and here it is turned into a beatitude for the avenger. The repetition in the Hebrew is the law of retaliation: the root גמל is in the noun 'your dealing' (גְּמוּלֵךְ) and again in the verb 'you dealt' (גָּמַלְתְּ), and the root שׁלם 'repay' sits between them: the act and its payment sound alike. Malbim notes that גְּמוּל is a deed done out of passion, love or hatred, and so the repayment is hatred for hatred. KJV 'rewardeth thee as thou hast served us' disguises that sound: 'reward' and 'served' are different words; the Hebrew has one root twice. The prayer is a plea for justice by those with no power, spoken in the ancient world where the vengeance of the weak was expressed as a prayer to God rather than an act.

philological_notes.note: Noun and verb from the same root: 'your dealing that you dealt'. Metzudat Zion notes that גמל can refer to the beginning of a harmful act (Joel 4:4), and Malbim that it means a deed done from emotion.

Passive participle, 'the devastated / plundered one'. Metzudat David and Radak read it as 'who will be devastated' by Darius; Malbim as already plundered by Cyrus; Metzudat Zion links it to plunder and robbery.
'How blessed / happy': the beatitude formula of Ps 1:1, applied here to the avenger.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [is] he who seizes and smashes your infants against the rock.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed is the one who takes your infants and breaks them against the rock.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hardest verse in the Psalter, and it must be played as it is written, not softened. The word עֹלָלַיִךְ means 'your nursing children', the suckling infants (Metzudat Zion cites Ps 8:3: 'infants and sucklings'). KJV 'little ones' blurs it, and 'against the stones' is wrong: the Hebrew has the singular 'the rock', הַסָּלַע, one hard surface. The verb is נָפַץ, 'to smash, shatter', the verb used of smashing jars (Judg 7:19, Metzudat Zion's example), and it is joined to 'seizes', a single, violent motion. The verse is a mirror, not an invention: the ancient world did this to conquered cities, and other prophets record the same fate for the children of conquered cities (Nah 3:10, Hos 14:1); Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as the same cruelty repaid in kind, and Meiri ties it to Isaiah 13:16-18, where God says through the prophet that the Medes will 'dash their infants to pieces'. Understand why it is here: the person speaking is powerless, with no army, and the only power to hand is the cry for justice, the lex talionis (eye for an eye) transferred to God. The psalm does not say the speaker will do it, only that the one who does is called 'blessed', the same word as the opening of the Psalter, which shocks as it is meant to. Ibn Ezra's comment gives the logic: the Babylonians smashed the infants of Israel, so the blessing falls on whoever repays that cruelty. Play it quietly, almost without volume: the horror lies in the plainness of the words, not in a shout. The reader is not asked to endorse the wish; the director should not let the actor make it a triumph. Later Jewish and Christian readers have taken it as an example of the honest anger of lament, an anger that is brought to God rather than acted on.

philological_notes.note: 'Your nursing children, your infants': the word is for babies and sucklings, not just 'little ones'. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'your small children', citing 'infants and sucklings' (Ps 8:3).

'And he smashes': the verb means shattering, scattering with force, as of jars (Judg 7:19). Metzudat Zion says it is 'breaking with crushing and scattering'. The tense is a perfect with vav, continuing 'who seizes'.
